overview.title: Rotation, scaling, linear and affine transforms as matrix products
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: Geometric meaning of the matrix product: rotation, scaling, general linear transforms, and the affine transform computed by a Dense layer
overview.central_idea: Multiplying a 2-D point by a 2 × 2 matrix rotates, scales or otherwise linearly transforms it; adding a translation vector on top gives an affine transform — which is exactly the `y = W @ x + b` computation of a `Dense` layer without activation.
overview.importance: This page closes the loop between the tensor operations of section 2.3 (matmul, addition) and their geometric meaning. Seeing the Dense layer as 'a linear map plus a shift' is the key that unlocks the next page's argument about why activation functions are indispensable, and the broader 'deep learning as geometric transformation' picture of section 2.3.6.
learning_objectives: Write the 2 × 2 matrix that rotates a 2-D vector counterclockwise by an angle θ and explain the role of each entry.
Recognize a diagonal matrix and explain why multiplying by one scales the horizontal and vertical axes independently.
State what a linear transform is and why rotation and scaling are special cases of it.
Define an affine transform as linear transform + translation and identify it with the Dense layer computation y = W @ x + b.
prerequisites: Tensor product / matmul and the `@` operator (p.56–57)
The Dense layer's computation output = relu(dot(input, W) + b) (p.52–53)

summary:
This page continues the list of elementary geometric operations that can be written as tensor operations, begun on p.60 with translation. Four items are covered, each as a bullet.

**Rotation.** A counterclockwise rotation of a 2-D vector by an angle θ is obtained by multiplying the vector by the 2 × 2 matrix `R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]`. Figure 2.10 shows a red square with the letter K being rotated by θ, with the matrix–vector product written above it.

**Scaling.** Vertical and horizontal scaling of an image is obtained by multiplying by a 2 × 2 *diagonal* matrix — a matrix whose only non-zero coefficients lie on the diagonal running from top left to bottom right. (The printed text says `S =` but the matrix itself is missing from the body; the matrix in Figure 2.11 is `[[1, 0], [0, -0.5]]`, which leaves x unchanged and multiplies y by −0.5, so the K is squashed to half height *and* flipped below the x-axis.)

**Linear transform.** A product with an *arbitrary* matrix implements a linear transform; rotation and scaling are, by definition, special cases of linear transforms.

**Affine transform.** An affine transform (Figure 2.12, on the next page) combines a linear transform (a matrix product) with a translation (a vector addition). The authors point out that this is exactly the `y = W @ x + b` computation implemented by a `Dense` layer: a `Dense` layer *without* an activation function is an affine layer.

The practical payoff is that every ingredient of the Dense layer now has a geometric reading — `W @ x` rotates/scales/shears the input space, `+ b` shifts it — which the next page (p.62) uses to show that stacking affine layers without activations collapses into a single affine layer, motivating nonlinear activations such as `relu`.

paragraphs.excerpt: Rotation—A counterclockwise rotation of a 2D vector by an angle theta
paragraphs.what_it_says: Rotating a 2-D vector counterclockwise by an angle θ is the same as multiplying it by the 2 × 2 matrix `R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]` (Figure 2.10).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The rotation is a matmul: the new coordinates are `x' = x·cos θ − y·sin θ` and `y' = x·sin θ + y·cos θ`. The two columns of R are where the unit vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) land after rotation — (cos θ, sin θ) and (−sin θ, cos θ). Because every point of the K is transformed by the same matrix, the whole shape turns rigidly around the origin without being stretched.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the first example on the page of a *matrix product* having a geometric meaning, in the same way that p.60 gave vector *addition* the meaning of translation. The Dense layer's `W @ x` is such a product, so this tells you what part of a Dense layer can do: it can turn the input space.
paragraphs.technical_idea: R is an orthogonal matrix with determinant 1: it preserves lengths and angles (`R.T @ R` is the identity). The rotation is counterclockwise for positive θ in the usual right-handed x–y axes; in image coordinates where y points down, the same matrix appears to rotate clockwise.

terminology.meaning: A 2 × 2 matrix of cosines and sines whose product with a vector turns the vector by a fixed angle around the origin.

connections: p.56–57: the tensor product (`matmul`, `@`) that is being used here was defined there.
p.60: translation was the vector-addition counterpart; rotation is the first matrix-product example.

paragraphs.excerpt: Scaling—A vertical and horizontal scaling of the image (see figure 2.11)
paragraphs.what_it_says: Scaling an image horizontally and vertically is done by multiplying by a 2 × 2 matrix S that is *diagonal*: its only non-zero coefficients lie on the diagonal from top left to bottom right. Figure 2.11 shows the example matrix `[[1, 0], [0, -0.5]]` applied to the K.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A diagonal matrix `[[s_x, 0], [0, s_y]]` multiplies x by s_x and y by s_y with no mixing between the axes: `S @ [x, y] = [s_x·x, s_y·y]`. In the figure s_x = 1 (width unchanged) and s_y = −0.5 (height halved and, because the sign is negative, the shape is mirrored across the x-axis — that is why the K sits upside-down below the axis).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Scaling is the second basic thing a matrix product can do to the input space: stretch or squash it along the axes. Together with rotation it gives intuition for what the learned weight matrix W of a Dense layer is doing to its inputs.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (not in the book): the body text reads `S =` and then nothing — the matrix was dropped in typesetting. The general form is the diagonal matrix above; the figure's matrix is the concrete instance. A negative diagonal entry is still a (signed) scaling; |s| < 1 shrinks, |s| > 1 enlarges, s < 0 also reflects.

terminology.meaning: A matrix whose entries off the main diagonal (top-left to bottom-right) are all zero; multiplying by it scales each coordinate independently.
Stretching or shrinking a shape along the coordinate axes by fixed factors.

connections: p.57: for a matrix–vector product each output coordinate is a dot product of a row of the matrix with the vector; with a diagonal row that dot product has only one surviving term.

paragraphs.excerpt: Linear transform—A product with an arbitrary matrix implements a linear transform.
paragraphs.what_it_says: A product with an arbitrary matrix implements a linear transform; scaling and rotation are, by definition, linear transforms.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Rotation and scaling matrices are just special cases. Any 2 × 2 matrix `[[a, b], [c, d]]` sends (x, y) to (a·x + b·y, c·x + d·y) — in general a combination of rotation, scaling and shearing. What all such maps share: they keep the origin fixed, map straight lines to straight lines, and keep parallel lines parallel.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It generalizes from the two tidy examples to the real situation in a Dense layer, where W is an arbitrary learned matrix — not a pure rotation or a pure scaling, but still a linear transform with the same geometric character.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a map f is linear when f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v) and f(c·u) = c·f(u). Every such map on vectors is a matrix product, and every matrix product is such a map — the two notions coincide.

terminology.meaning: A map of the form x ↦ W @ x: it preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication and always keeps the origin in place.

connections: p.52–53: the Dense layer's `dot(input, W)` is exactly such an arbitrary-matrix product.

paragraphs.excerpt: Affine transform—An affine transform (see figure 2.12) is the combination of
paragraphs.what_it_says: An affine transform (Figure 2.12, next page) is a linear transform (matrix product) followed by a translation (vector addition). The authors note that this is exactly the `y = W @ x + b` computation of a `Dense` layer, so a `Dense` layer without an activation function is an affine layer.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The two tensor operations studied geometrically so far — matmul and addition — compose into one named operation. Geometrically, `W @ x` rotates/scales/shears the input around the origin, then `+ b` slides the result to a new location. Everything a Dense layer does before its activation is of this form.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the punchline of the subsection: the layer you met in chapter 2's MNIST example is nothing more mysterious than 'turn, stretch, shift'. It also sets up p.62, where the authors show that composing affine transforms yields another affine transform, so Dense layers without activations cannot build anything beyond a single affine map — the reason `relu` is needed.
paragraphs.technical_idea: An affine map does not in general fix the origin (b moves it), so it is *not* linear in the strict sense — hence the separate name.

terminology.meaning: A linear transform followed by a translation: x ↦ W @ x + b.
A Dense layer with no activation; it computes only W @ x + b.

connections: p.52–53: `output = relu(dot(input, W) + b)` — drop the relu and you have this affine map.
p.62: composition of two affine transforms and why activations are needed.
p.60: translation (`+ b`) as vector addition.

concepts.name: Rotation matrix
concepts.definition: The 2 × 2 matrix `[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]` whose product with a 2-D vector rotates it counterclockwise by θ about the origin.
concepts.intuition: Its columns are where the two axis unit vectors end up after turning by θ; any point is a mix of those two unit vectors, so it turns the same way.
concepts.technical: Orthogonal (R.T @ R = I) with determinant 1, so lengths and angles are preserved. Rotations compose by adding angles: R(α) @ R(β) = R(α + β).
concepts.significance: The first example on this page of a matrix product with a direct geometric reading; shows that a Dense layer's W can turn the input space.
concepts.misconception: That the rotation turns the vector clockwise — with standard axes (y up) and positive θ it is counterclockwise, as the book says.

concepts.name: Scaling (diagonal) matrix
concepts.definition: A diagonal 2 × 2 matrix `[[s_x, 0], [0, s_y]]`; multiplying by it scales the x coordinate by s_x and the y coordinate by s_y.
concepts.intuition: No mixing between axes — each coordinate is simply multiplied by its own factor, like stretching an image with independent width and height handles.
concepts.technical: A matrix is 'diagonal' when its only non-zero coefficients lie on the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal. Negative factors reflect; factors with |s| < 1 shrink. Figure 2.11 uses [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]].
concepts.significance: The second geometric reading of a matrix product; with rotation it builds intuition for what an arbitrary W can do.
concepts.example: [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] @ [2, 4] = [2, −2]: width kept, height halved and flipped.
concepts.misconception: That scaling always enlarges or keeps orientation — a negative diagonal entry mirrors the shape, as in Figure 2.11.

concepts.name: Linear transform
concepts.definition: A map implemented by a product with an arbitrary matrix: x ↦ W @ x.
concepts.intuition: Grid lines stay straight, parallel and evenly spaced, and the origin never moves; rotation, scaling and shearing are all of this kind.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: f is linear iff f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v) and f(c·u) = c·f(u); on finite-dimensional vectors every linear map is a matrix product and vice versa.
concepts.significance: The general case of the matrix product in a Dense layer: W is an arbitrary learned matrix, so `W @ x` is a general linear transform.
concepts.example: [[1, 1], [0, 1]] is a shear: it slides points sideways in proportion to their height.
concepts.misconception: That a linear transform can move the origin — it cannot; that requires the translation part of an affine transform.

concepts.name: Affine transform
concepts.definition: A linear transform (matrix product) combined with a translation (vector addition): y = W @ x + b.
concepts.intuition: Turn/stretch the shape around the origin, then slide it somewhere else.
concepts.technical: Exactly the computation of a Dense layer without activation. The affine image of a straight line is a straight line and parallelism is preserved, but the origin generally moves.
concepts.significance: Identifies the Dense layer with a well-understood geometric object and sets up the argument (p.62) that stacking affine layers without activations gives only another affine map.
concepts.misconception: That `W @ x + b` is 'linear' — strictly it is affine; the `+ b` breaks linearity because the origin is not fixed.

concepts.name: Dense layer (as an affine layer)
concepts.definition: A layer computing output = activation(W @ input + b); without activation it is an affine layer.
concepts.intuition: A Dense layer is a geometric transform of the input space — a linear part learned in W, a shift learned in b, and (when present) a nonlinear 'bend' from the activation.
concepts.technical: W has shape (input_dim, output_dim) in Keras' convention (`dot(input, W)` on p.52) while the geometric presentation here writes it as `W @ x`; either way the computation is the same affine map.
concepts.significance: Reframes the layer from chapter 2's MNIST example as rotation/scaling/translation of data points.
concepts.example: The 512-unit Dense layer of the MNIST model maps a 784-dimensional point to a 512-dimensional one via an affine transform followed by relu.
concepts.misconception: That the `Dense` layer's power lies in W @ x + b alone — without the activation, any stack of such layers is a single affine map (p.62).

math.title: Counterclockwise rotation by θ as a matrix product
math.latex: R = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}, \qquad R \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x\cos\theta - y\sin\theta \\ x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta \end{bmatrix}
math.source_text: R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]  (and in Figure 2.10 the matrix is shown multiplied by the column vector [x, y])

variables.meaning: Coordinates of the point (vector) being rotated.

math.operations: A matrix–vector product (matmul). Each output coordinate is the dot product of one row of R with the vector [x, y].
math.purpose: Shows that a rigid rotation — a purely geometric operation — is a tensor operation of the kind a Dense layer performs.
math.interpretation: The columns of R, (cos θ, sin θ) and (−sin θ, cos θ), are the images of the unit vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1). Any point is x times the first unit vector plus y times the second, so it is carried to x times the first column plus y times the second column.
math.intuition: Think of a compass needle at angle 0 being turned by θ: its tip (1, 0) ends at (cos θ, sin θ). The whole plane turns with it.
math.numerical_example: θ = 90° (cos θ = 0, sin θ = 1): R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Then R @ [2, 1] = [0·2 − 1·1, 1·2 + 0·1] = [−1, 2] — the point has turned a quarter-circle counterclockwise. With θ = 30° (cos ≈ 0.866, sin = 0.5): R @ [1, 0] = [0.866, 0.5].

math.title: Scaling by a diagonal matrix (Figure 2.11)
math.latex: S = \begin{bmatrix} s_x & 0 \\ 0 & s_y \end{bmatrix}, \qquad S \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} s_x x \\ s_y y \end{bmatrix}; \qquad \text{Figure 2.11: } \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -0.5 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ -0.5\,y \end{bmatrix}
math.source_text: S =  (matrix missing in the running text); Figure 2.11 shows [[1, 0], [0, -0.5]] • [x, y]

variables.meaning: Horizontal and vertical scale factors (the diagonal coefficients). In the figure s_x = 1 and s_y = −0.5.
Coordinates of the point being scaled.

math.operations: Matrix–vector product with a diagonal matrix: because the off-diagonal entries are 0, each output coordinate is just its input coordinate times one factor.
math.purpose: Shows that stretching or shrinking along the axes is also a matmul, and introduces the term 'diagonal matrix'.
math.interpretation: The general form is the book's definition (only the diagonal is non-zero). The figure's instance keeps x, halves y and flips its sign — the K ends up half as tall and mirrored below the x-axis. Note (not in the book): the general form is reconstructed here because the printed text omits the matrix after `S =`.
math.intuition: Like dragging the height handle of an image to 50% — and then dragging it past zero so the picture flips.
math.numerical_example: [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] @ [2, 4] = [1·2 + 0·4, 0·2 + (−0.5)·4] = [2, −2]. The top-right corner of a K drawn in the first quadrant moves below the axis.

math.title: Affine transform = the Dense layer without activation
math.latex: y = W x + b \quad\text{(book: } y = W @ x + b\text{)}

variables.meaning: Input vector (a point in the input space).
Weight matrix: the linear part (rotation/scaling/shear) of the transform.

math.operations: A tensor product (`W @ x`) followed by a vector addition (`+ b`) — the two operations given geometric meaning on p.59–61.
math.purpose: Names the combination of linear transform and translation and identifies it with the computation of a `Dense` layer; a Dense layer without activation is an affine layer.
math.interpretation: First the space is linearly deformed about the origin by W, then every point is shifted by the same vector b. The origin is generally moved, which is what distinguishes 'affine' from 'linear'.
math.intuition: Turn and stretch the sheet of paper, then slide it across the table.

math.title: What makes a transform linear (not in the book)
math.latex: f(u + v) = f(u) + f(v), \qquad f(c\,u) = c\,f(u) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad f(x) = W x
math.source_text: The book only says 'a product with an arbitrary matrix implements a linear transform'; this characterization is added.

variables.meaning: The transform (a function from vectors to vectors).

math.operations: Two defining properties: additivity and homogeneity. Together they are equivalent to 'f is a matrix product'.
math.purpose: Explains why rotation and scaling are 'by definition' linear and why adding b breaks linearity: f(0) = W @ 0 = 0 for any linear f, but an affine f(0) = b ≠ 0.
math.interpretation: Linear maps are those that respect the vector-space structure; geometrically they keep the origin fixed and keep grid lines straight, parallel and evenly spaced.
math.intuition: Doubling the input doubles the output; adding inputs adds outputs. A shift by b violates both (doubling x does not double x + b).

deeper.title: Why the rotation matrix has that shape — follow the unit vectors
deeper.body:
1. Any 2-D point is a combination of the two axis unit vectors: `[x, y] = x·[1, 0] + y·[0, 1]`.
2. A matrix product is linear, so `R @ [x, y] = x·(R @ [1, 0]) + y·(R @ [0, 1])` — the image of a point is the same combination of the images of the unit vectors.
3. `R @ [1, 0]` is the **first column** of R, and `R @ [0, 1]` is the **second column**.
4. Rotating `[1, 0]` counterclockwise by θ puts it at `[cos θ, sin θ]` (basic trigonometry on the unit circle). Rotating `[0, 1]` — which is 90° further round — gives `[cos(θ+90°), sin(θ+90°)] = [−sin θ, cos θ]`.
5. Stack those two results as columns: `R = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]` — the book's matrix.

The same recipe explains the scaling matrix: `[1, 0] ↦ [s_x, 0]` and `[0, 1] ↦ [0, s_y]`, giving the diagonal matrix. And it explains the 'arbitrary matrix = linear transform' bullet: *any* 2 × 2 matrix is just a choice of where the two unit vectors go.

deeper.title: Reading the sign in Figure 2.11
deeper.body:
The matrix in Figure 2.11 is `[[1, 0], [0, −0.5]]`. Take the four corners of a square K in the first quadrant: `(0, 0), (2, 0), (2, 2), (0, 2)`.

| corner | x' = 1·x + 0·y | y' = 0·x + (−0.5)·y |
|---|---|---|
| (0, 0) | 0 | 0 |
| (2, 0) | 2 | 0 |
| (2, 2) | 2 | −1 |
| (0, 2) | 0 | −1 |

The width (0 → 2) is unchanged, the height has gone from 2 to 1, and the shape now hangs *below* the x-axis — exactly the half-height, upside-down K drawn in the figure. Had the entry been +0.5 the K would be squashed but still upright. So 'scaling' with a negative factor includes a reflection; the book's figure shows this even though the text does not comment on it.

deeper.title: The Dense layer as a geometric machine
deeper.body:
Picture the input data as dots drawn on a transparent sheet. A `Dense` layer without activation does two things to the sheet: first it deforms it linearly around a pin at the origin (`W @ x` — the sheet can be rotated, stretched along some directions, squashed along others, or sheared), and then it slides the whole sheet across the table (`+ b`). The learned weights decide *how much* to turn, stretch and slide.

What the layer cannot do, no matter the weights, is *bend* the sheet: straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel. That limitation is why the next page (p.62) brings in `relu` — the activation is what lets a layer fold the sheet.

deeper.title: Rotation in a 784-dimensional space?
deeper.body: The page draws everything in 2-D, but the MNIST Dense layer from p.41–44 multiplies a 784-dimensional input by a 784 × 512 weight matrix. Nothing changes conceptually: the product is still a linear transform that can rotate some directions, scale others and project the data down to 512 dimensions, and `+ b` still translates it. We simply cannot draw it. Section 2.3.6 (p.62) builds on exactly this: a neural network is a chain of such geometric steps in a high-dimensional space.

Here W is a 90° rotation and b = [1, 0.25] (the translation vector from p.59); toggle the translation to see the difference between linear (origin fixed) and affine (origin moves).

misconceptions.correction: With standard axes (x right, y up) and positive θ, `[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]` rotates counterclockwise, as the book states. A clockwise rotation uses −θ (which flips the sign of the two sine entries).

misconceptions.claim: Scaling can only make a shape bigger or smaller; it cannot flip it.
misconceptions.correction: A diagonal entry can be negative. Figure 2.11's matrix has −0.5 for y, which halves the height *and* mirrors the shape across the x-axis — that is why the K appears upside-down.

misconceptions.claim: Because a Dense layer computes W @ x + b, it is a linear transform.
misconceptions.correction: It is an *affine* transform: linear part W @ x plus a translation b. Linear transforms keep the origin fixed; the `+ b` moves it. The book is careful to use the word 'affine' for the Dense layer without activation.

misconceptions.claim: Rotation and scaling are different kinds of operation from 'a matrix product'.
misconceptions.correction: They are special cases: any matrix product is a linear transform, and the rotation and diagonal matrices are particular matrices. The book says they are linear transforms 'by definition'.

takeaways: A counterclockwise rotation by θ is the matrix product with R = [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
Scaling along the axes is the product with a diagonal matrix (non-zero entries only on the top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal); Figure 2.11 uses [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]], which also flips the shape.
A product with any matrix is a linear transform; rotation and scaling are special cases.
Linear transform + translation = affine transform, and that is exactly y = W @ x + b — a Dense layer without activation is an affine layer.
Matmul and addition, the two tensor operations of a Dense layer, therefore have clean geometric meanings: deform about the origin, then shift.

questions.question: Which matrix rotates a 2-D vector counterclockwise by an angle θ, according to the page?
options: [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]
questions.explanation: The book gives R = [[cos(theta), -sin(theta)], [sin(theta), cos(theta)]]. The second option is its transpose, which rotates *clockwise* by θ. The third scrambles the entries and is not a rotation. The fourth is diagonal — a scaling, not a rotation.

questions.question: Apply Figure 2.11's scaling matrix [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] to the point [4, 6]. What do you get, and what happened geometrically?
questions.answer: [4, −3]: the x coordinate is unchanged, the y coordinate is halved and its sign flipped (mirrored across the x-axis).
questions.explanation: Row 1 · [4, 6] = 1·4 + 0·6 = 4; row 2 · [4, 6] = 0·4 + (−0.5)·6 = −3. A diagonal matrix scales each axis independently; the negative factor on y both shrinks and reflects, which is why the K in Figure 2.11 is upside-down and half as tall.

questions.question: What is a 'diagonal matrix', and why does multiplying by one perform scaling rather than rotation?
questions.answer: A matrix whose only non-zero coefficients lie on the diagonal from top left to bottom right. Because the off-diagonal entries are zero, each output coordinate equals its input coordinate times one factor — the axes never mix, so points move along the axes (stretch/shrink) instead of turning.
questions.explanation: The book defines the term in the Scaling bullet. Rotation requires mixing x into y and y into x (the sine terms), which needs non-zero off-diagonal entries.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a linear transform and an affine transform, and say which one a Dense layer without activation computes.
questions.answer: A linear transform is a product with a matrix, x ↦ W @ x; it keeps the origin fixed. An affine transform adds a translation: x ↦ W @ x + b, which can move the origin. A Dense layer without activation computes y = W @ x + b, so it is an affine transform (an 'affine layer').
questions.explanation: The page states that a product with an arbitrary matrix is a linear transform and that an affine transform combines such a product with a vector addition — 'exactly the y = W @ x + b computation implemented by the Dense layer'.

questions.question: Why can the authors say rotation and scaling are linear transforms 'by definition'?
options: Because both are implemented as a product with a matrix, and any matrix product is a linear transform
Because both preserve the lengths of vectors
Because both involve a translation vector
questions.answer: Because both are implemented as a product with a matrix, and any matrix product is a linear transform
questions.explanation: The bullet says 'A product with an arbitrary matrix implements a linear transform' — rotation and scaling are just particular matrices. Scaling does not preserve lengths (so the second option is wrong), neither involves a translation (that would make them affine), and only rotation uses trigonometric functions.

questions.question: Using the rotation matrix with θ = 90°, rotate the point [3, 1]. Then apply an affine transform with the same W and b = [1, 0.25]. Give both results.
questions.explanation: For θ = 90°, cos θ = 0 and sin θ = 1, so R = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]. Row 1: 0·3 + (−1)·1 = −1; row 2: 1·3 + 0·1 = 3. The affine transform then adds the translation vector element-wise — the linear part followed by a translation, exactly as the page defines it.

questions.question: Can you, without looking, (a) write the rotation matrix for an angle θ, (b) sketch what [[1, 0], [0, −0.5]] does to a shape in the first quadrant, and (c) say in one sentence why a Dense layer without activation is 'affine'?
questions.answer: (a) [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]; (b) same width, half the height, flipped below the x-axis; (c) it computes a matrix product (linear transform) plus a bias vector (translation), which is the definition of an affine transform.
questions.explanation: These three items are the page's core content: Figure 2.10's matrix, Figure 2.11's matrix, and the final bullet's identification of y = W @ x + b with an affine transform. If any part is shaky, re-read the corresponding bullet and try the vector_geometry widget.
